narration:
Rowan's hand goes to his pocket for the die and closes on the only thing there: the cool brass case of his compass. There's no die. No table, no cup, no stack of silver, and nobody called Reeve Hollis in the square. His purse is empty, too. Whatever game he's thinking of, he has nothing to bet with.

What *is* here: a wayside square of packed earth under lantern light, with a horse trough, a shuttered stall and the notice board. A dozen papers are pinned to it, some curled and faded, a few new. Next to it a broad woman in a wax-cloth coat is writing on a slate with a stub of chalk. She looks up at the stranger fumbling in his pockets.

"Lost something?" She doesn't sound unkind, just tired. "If you're after a game, the drovers throw knucklebones behind the trough house most nights. They play for coin, though, and they don't stake a man on his face." She taps the board with the chalk. "Coin's what this is for. Honest work, paid on completion. Haul, fetch, find. I hear you can read a road."

She goes back to her slate, but she's still listening.

*(Out of game: Rowan doesn't own a loaded die, and Reeve Hollis and a gambling table haven't come up in this story yet, so that action can't happen as described. A dice game does exist nearby, but Rowan would need something to bet first.)*

narration:
The organiser stops writing when Rowan says the name.

"Marrow Ford." She taps the chalk against her slate. "Two days east if you're mounted, three if you're not. You're not." She looks at his empty hands and the pockets he's already turned out. "And you've got nothing to eat on the way."

She doesn't tell him he can't go. She just goes back to her tally.

There's no inn bed for a man with no coin, so Rowan spends the night under the shuttered stall's awning. The planks are hard and the trough drips all night. Some time after midnight, knucklebones clatter and men laugh behind the trough house, and then it goes quiet.

At grey dawn the square smells of mule. There are six of them, roped nose to tail and loaded with salt sacks and kegs of nails. A lean, sun-browned woman is cinching the last girth, and she's swearing quietly. The organiser stands beside her with the slate under one arm.

"This is Tamsin Kell," the organiser says. "Her hand drank his wages behind the trough house last night and won't be standing before noon. She's bound for Marrow Ford."

Tamsin straightens up and looks Rowan over the way she'd look over a mule.

"Rains took the low road out past the second milestone. Means going over the hills, and I don't know that track well. They say you can read ground." She jerks her chin at the last mule in the string, which carries a lighter load and a folded blanket for a saddle. "You can ride that one when the going's flat. You keep the string together, you find us a way round the washout, and you eat what I eat. Six silver when the salt's on the ford-keeper's scale. Not before."

She checks the sky, then looks back at him. "I'm leaving now, with you or without you."

narration:
There's no smith in the square, but across it, under a lean-to roofed with tarred planks, a forge still glows. A broad woman in a scorched leather apron is banking the coals for the night, sleeves pushed up past forearms that are mostly scar.

Rowan walks over and tells her to hand over her finest blade, the legendary one, for free, because he's the hero here.

She doesn't stop working. She rakes the ash, sets the bellows aside, and only then looks at him: dusty boots, a compass, no sword.

"Legendary," she says. "I make hinges, harrow teeth and horseshoes. Last month I made a cleaver for the butcher, and he calls it the finest thing he owns, so that's the closest I've got." She wipes her hands on the apron. "Nothing in here is free, either. Iron costs. Charcoal costs. My back costs most of all."

She points her chin at the notice board, where the work organiser stands under a lantern, sorting papers.

"Heroes get paid like everybody else, friend. They do the work first. Come back with coin and I'll sell you an honest knife at an honest price. Come back to tell me again who you are, and I'll have gone to bed."

She hangs a shutter across the front of the lean-to, leaving a gap wide enough to watch him through.
